# Overview {.unnumbered}
::: {.grid .mt-3 .mb-4}


::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-9}
[Learn how to turn gridded biodiversity data into an EBVCube: a reusable file that can be checked, shared and published through the EBV Data Portal.]{.lead}
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**New to this?** \
Eight units take you from the EBV framework and EBVCube concepts to creating,
validating and publishing a dataset. [Unit 1 — Introduction](01-introduction.qmd)
introduces the terminology used throughout the tutorial; if you already know the
EBV framework, you can jump straight to any unit below.

[R ≥ 4.2 · 3.3 MB example download · no prior netCDF experience needed]{.small .text-muted}
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Four names to keep separate"}
An **Essential Biodiversity Variable (EBV)** is a standardised measurement used to describe and track an important aspect of biodiversity. An **EBVCube** is the standardised file that stores gridded EBV data and the information needed to interpret it. **`ebvcube`** is the R package used to inspect, read, visualise and create EBVCubes. The **EBV Data Portal** is the online service where datasets can be discovered, submitted, published and explored.
:::


## Four dimensions, one file

::: {.grid}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-5}
![](images/ebvcube-hero-preview.png){fig-alt="An EBVCube shown as three stacked boxes, one per entity: All birds, Forest birds and Non-forest birds. The front face of each box is a world map, with longitude running horizontally and latitude vertically; time runs back along the depth axis."}
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-7}
EBVCubes use netCDF, a file format designed for multidimensional scientific data. The format keeps data values, their geographic and temporal coordinates, and descriptive metadata together in one self-describing file. It follows the Climate and Forecast (**CF**) and Attribute Convention for Data Discovery (**ACDD**) conventions, plus **EBVCube-specific** biodiversity terms. This common structure makes datasets easier to discover, interpret and exchange.

The figure uses the tutorial's bird-diversity example to illustrate this structure. Each box represents one biological entity. It contains values on the same global grid, with time running along the depth axis.


::: {.grid}

::: {.g-col-6 .border .rounded .p-3}
**Longitude** (`lon`)

[The east–west coordinate of the spatial grid. Its values are determined by the spatial `extent` and `resolution` of your data.]{.small .text-muted}
:::


::: {.g-col-6 .border .rounded .p-3}
**Latitude** (`lat`)

[The north–south coordinate of the spatial grid. Every layer added to the cube must use the same grid and coordinate reference system.]{.small .text-muted}
:::


::: {.g-col-6 .border .rounded .p-3}
**Time** (`time`)

[The date or dates represented by the data. The values declared in the metadata must match the layers you add to the cube.]{.small .text-muted}
:::

::: {.g-col-6 .border .rounded .p-3}
**Entity** (`entity`)

[The biological unit represented by the data: for example, a species, a group of species, or an ecosystem type.]{.small .text-muted}

:::

:::

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Metrics** and **scenarios** are not dimensions. They organise the four-dimensional data cubes inside an EBVCube.

A **metric** is what is measured, for example species richness, the relative change in species richness, or its uncertainty. Each metric group contains one four-dimensional data array named `ebv_cube`, with the dimensions `lon`, `lat`, `time` and `entity`.

A **scenario** is an optional higher-level group, normally used for projected data. For example, the same metric may be modelled under several alternative future land-use pathways. When scenarios are present, each metric is stored separately within each scenario: `scenario_1/metric_1/ebv_cube`.

If a dataset has 3 scenarios and 3 metrics, it therefore contains 9 scenario–metric
combinations and 9 `ebv_cube` data arrays. All of these cubes use the same four-dimensional
structure.
:::


## From concepts to publication

First, you learn the terms and file structure. You then prepare and validate an EBVCube locally in R, and use the portal to publish it. Metadata can be prepared either through the portal form or in R; both routes produce the same JSON file used to create the EBVCube.

```{mermaid}

%%{init: {"flowchart": {"htmlLabels": false}} }%%
flowchart LR
  A("Unit 1<br/>Understand EBVs and EBVCubes")
  B("Units 2–5<br/>Create and validate an EBVCube in R")
  C("Unit 6<br/>Publish on the EBV Data Portal")

  classDef concept fill:#E8F1F8,stroke:#4E7894,color:#12211F

```

## One real dataset, start to finish

This published dataset illustrates how an EBVCube stores several scenarios and metrics. The later units identify the exact example inputs used in their code; the same creation workflow can be applied to your own data.


::: {.callout-note}
## Global trends in biodiversity (BES-SIM cSAR-iDiv)

[id = 30]{.badge .bg-secondary}
[Community composition]{.badge .bg-secondary}
[3 entities]{.badge .bg-secondary}
[3 metrics]{.badge .bg-secondary}
[3 scenarios]{.badge .bg-secondary}
[1900 · 2015 · 2050]{.badge .bg-secondary}

Bird species richness on a 1° global grid, modelled with cSAR-iDiv for all birds,
forest birds and non-forest birds, under three SSP-RCP land-use scenarios. Roughly
3.3 MB, downloaded once and cached locally.

*Martins, I., Pereira, H. (2022).*
[Dataset page](https://portal.geobon.org/ebv-detail?id=30) ·
DOI [10.25829/5zmy41](https://doi.org/10.25829/5zmy41)

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(ebvcube)

ebv_download(id = 30, outputdir = tempdir(), overwrite = FALSE)
```

Keep this example in mind as you learn the workflow: its nine scenario–metric combinations show how several four-dimensional data cubes can coexist in one file. To create your *own* EBVCube, replace the example metadata and data where the units indicate. Your entities, metrics, scenarios, dimensions and metadata may differ.

:::

## Before you start

::: {.grid}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
You do not need prior knowledge of EBVs, netCDF files or the EBV Data Portal. [Unit 1](01-introduction.qmd) introduces the concepts and vocabulary used throughout the tutorial.

It helps to be comfortable with:

-   basic R: installing packages and running scripts;
-   basic geospatial data handling in R, using packages such as `terra`;
-   biodiversity raster data, if you want to create your own EBVCube rather than follow the example.


A free [GEO BON account](https://members.geobon.org/register/index) is needed if you use the portal's metadata form or submit a dataset for publication. It is not needed to read public datasets or follow the R-only metadata workflow.
:::


::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
**Key resources**

-   [EBV Data Portal](https://portal.geobon.org/) — discover, download and publish EBV datasets.
-   [`ebvcube` on GitHub](https://github.com/EBVcube/ebvcube) — also on [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ebvcube) and the [b-cubed r-universe](https://b-cubed-eu.r-universe.dev/ebvcube).
-   [Package documentation](https://EBVcube.github.io/ebvcube/) — the full function reference this tutorial builds on.
-   [Format specification](https://github.com/EBVcube/EBVCube-format) — the structural rules behind the format.
-   [GEO BON — what are EBVs?](https://geobon.org/ebvs/what-are-ebvs/) — the canonical definition and the six classes.
-   [Quoss et al. (2022)](https://biss.pensoft.net/article/91215/) — the methods paper describing the package.
:::

:::
